title: Perimeter as Boundary Arc Length
content: Defines the perimeter of a convex body K as the planar arc length of a closed C¹ parametrisation γ : [a,b] → ℝ² of its boundary ∂K. By reusing the parent file's planarArcLength, the perimeter inherits all of the arc-length machinery already verified for the smooth-noodle theorem, so no new analytic content is introduced at this step.
mathContext: $\mathrm{perimeter}(K) = \int_a^b \lVert \gamma'(t)\rVert\, dt$ for a closed C¹ parametrisation $\gamma$ of $\partial K$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$.

title: Perimeter Is Nonnegative
content: The perimeter is nonnegative because it is the integral of a nonnegative integrand (a square root) over an interval with a ≤ b. The proof unfolds the definition and applies intervalIntegral.integral_nonneg with the pointwise bound Real.sqrt_nonneg. This is a sign-structure lemma needed downstream for the cut-line nonnegativity result.
mathContext: $0 \le \int_a^b \sqrt{(\partial_t\gamma_1)^2 + (\partial_t\gamma_2)^2}\, dt$ since the integrand is $\ge 0$ and $a \le b$.

title: Buffon's Coin — Boundary Crossings
content: The central result: for a convex body whose boundary is a closed C¹ curve, the expected number of crossings of ∂K with a parallel line grid of spacing d is 2·perimeter/(πd). The proof is a single application of the parent's main theorem buffon_smooth_of_contDiff to the boundary curve — the entire analytic computation is reused, so the coin result costs essentially one line. The closure hypothesis γ a = γ b is what makes planarArcLength the full perimeter of the closed boundary; it is not needed for the formula itself (hence the underscore).
mathContext: $\mathbb{E}[\#\{\text{crossings of }\partial K\}] = \dfrac{2\,p}{\pi d}$, where $p$ is the perimeter — independent of the shape of $K$.

title: Cut Lines via the Convex 0-or-2 Dichotomy
content: Defines the expected number of grid lines that cut K as half the expected boundary-crossing count. This factor of two is the ONLY place convexity enters the development: a line meeting a convex body crosses its boundary in exactly 0 or 2 points, so each cutting line contributes two crossings. Because Mathlib v4.26.0 has no convex-geometry bearer for the 0/2 intersection fact and concreteSmoothExpectedCrossings is an integral model rather than a literal point count, the halving is encoded definitionally rather than derived — an honest accounting of where the convex hypothesis is used.
mathContext: $\mathbb{E}[\#\text{cut lines}] := \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}[\#\text{boundary crossings}]$; a line meets a convex $\partial K$ in $0$ or $2$ points.

title: Buffon's Coin — Expected Cut Lines
content: Combines the boundary-crossing formula with the factor-of-two definition to give the expected number of grid lines cutting K as perimeter/(πd). The proof unfolds expectedLineCuts, rewrites with the boundary-crossing theorem, and closes with ring. This is the form in which Buffon's coin is most often quoted: the average number of grid lines meeting the body equals its perimeter divided by πd.

title: The Coin: Circle Parametrisation
content: The canonical convex body — a disk of radius r with boundary t ↦ (r cos t, r sin t) on [0, 2π]. Two structural facts are established: the parametrisation is C¹ (discharged by fun_prop from smoothness of sin and cos) and it is closed (γ 0 = γ 2π, via cos/sin at 0 and 2π). Together these verify that the circle satisfies the hypotheses of the general Buffon's-coin theorems.

title: Component Derivatives of the Circle
content: Computes the coordinate derivatives of the circle parametrisation: d/dt(r cos t) = -r sin t and d/dt(r sin t) = r cos t. Each follows from Mathlib's hasDerivAt_cos / hasDerivAt_sin scaled by the constant r via const_mul. These feed directly into the arc-length integrand used to compute the perimeter.

title: Circle Perimeter Equals 2πr
content: Proves that the disk of radius r has perimeter 2πr by evaluating the arc-length integral. The key step shows the integrand √((-r sin t)² + (r cos t)²) collapses to the constant r, using the Pythagorean identity sin²+cos² = 1 and √(r²) = r for r ≥ 0. The integral of the constant r over [0, 2π] is then 2π·r. This is the one genuinely analytic computation specific to the circle.
mathContext: $\int_0^{2\pi} \sqrt{(-r\sin t)^2 + (r\cos t)^2}\, dt = \int_0^{2\pi} r\, dt = 2\pi r$, using $\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t = 1$.

title: Coin Boundary Crossings Equal 4r/d
content: Instantiates the general boundary-crossing formula on the circle: substituting perimeter 2πr into 2p/(πd) and simplifying with field_simp gives 4r/d. This is the expected number of times a dropped coin's edge crosses the grid lines.

title: Laplace's Classical Buffon's-Coin Result: 2r/d
content: The headline classical result: a coin of radius r cuts an expected 2r/d grid lines, obtained by halving the 4r/d crossing count. For r ≤ d/2 (diameter at most the line spacing) the coin meets at most one line, so this expectation equals the probability of meeting a line — exactly diameter/d, Laplace's 1812 answer to Buffon's coin problem.

title: Shape Independence
content: Two convex bodies of equal perimeter cut the same expected number of grid lines, no matter how different their shapes. The proof simply rewrites both sides with the cut-line formula perimeter/(πd) and uses the equal-perimeter hypothesis. This captures the most striking feature of Buffon's coin: only the perimeter matters — a circle, a smoothed square, and an ellipse of the same perimeter all behave identically.
mathContext: $p_1 = p_2 \implies \dfrac{p_1}{\pi d} = \dfrac{p_2}{\pi d}$, so the expected cut counts coincide.

title: Monotonicity in Perimeter
content: A convex body with longer perimeter cuts at least as many expected grid lines (at fixed spacing). The proof rewrites both sides with the cut-line formula and applies div_le_div_of_nonneg_right since πd > 0, reducing the claim to the perimeter inequality hypothesis. Together with shape independence this fully characterises the expected cut count as an increasing function of perimeter alone.
